```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)    
library(ggplot2)
library(car)      
library(mgcv)
library(e1071)    
library(caret) 

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
          theme(plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5)))

group_cols <- c(near = "#0072B2", far = "#E69F00")
```

# Introduction

# Data Sources

```{r data-import, include=FALSE}
swiss_hotel_panel <- read_csv("data/processed/swiss_hotel_panel.csv")
```

# Data Preparation

```{r data-check-na}
hotel <- read_csv("data/processed/swiss_hotel_panel.csv")
hotel |> filter(is.na(arrivals)) |> select(year, canton, origin_country)
hotel <- hotel |> filter(!is.na(arrivals))
```
The BFS does not publish two values, namely Appenzell Innerrhoden, GCC and South Korea, 2022. We drop these two rows, which leaves `r nrow(hotel)` rows: 26 cantons × 12 origin markets × 10 years.

```{r prep}
hotel <- hotel |>
  mutate(
    canton         = factor(canton),
    origin_country = factor(origin_country),
    origin_group   = factor(origin_group, levels = c("near", "far")),
    covid_period   = factor(covid_period, levels = c("pre", "during", "post")),
    log_arrivals   = log1p(arrivals),
    log_beds       = log(beds)
  )
```

The text columns become factors, with "near" for the orign group and "pre" for the covid period as reference levels. `log_arrivals` and `log_beds` are explained in the next section.

# Data Exploration

## Response: arrivals

```{r eda-arrivals, fig.height = 5, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%"}
ggplot(hotel, aes(arrivals)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Arrivals: very right-skewed", x = "Arrivals per canton, market and year", y = "Number of rows")

ggplot(hotel, aes(log_arrivals)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey60", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "log(arrivals + 1): more symmetric", x = "log(arrivals + 1)", y = "Number of rows")
```

Arrivals are an amount and very right-skewed, ranging from 0 to about 500,000, while most rows are a few thousand. On the log scale the distribution is roughly symmetric, so models use `log_arrivals = log(arrivals + 1)`. The `+ 1` is needed for the `r sum(hotel$arrivals == 0)` rows with zero arrivals. On the log scale, effects read as percentage changes. For the same reason, hotel beds are also used on the log scale (`log_beds`).

## Response: growth

The binary response of the GLM and the SVM, `growth`, is 1 if a market had more arrivals in a canton than in the year before (2015 is used for 2016) and 0 otherwise. It is also missing in two more rows, the 2023 values of the same two cells, because there is no 2022 value to compare with.

```{r data-check-na-growth}
hotel |> filter(is.na(growth)) |> select(year, canton, origin_country)
```

These two rows have a valid number of arrivals, so we keep them for the LM and the GAM. The GLM and the SVM leave them out, which leaves `r sum(!is.na(hotel$growth))` rows for those models.

```{r eda-growth, fig.height = 5, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%"}
growth.data <- hotel |> filter(!is.na(growth))

growth.data |>
  group_by(year, origin_group) |>
  summarise(share = mean(growth), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, colour = origin_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2025) +   
  labs(title = "Share of rows with growth", x = NULL, y = "Share with growth",
       colour = "Market")

# binomial smoother, so the curve stays between 0 and 1
ggplot(growth.data, aes(gdp_growth_origin, growth, colour = origin_group)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x), method.args = list(family = binomial)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  labs(title = "Growth vs GDP growth of origin", x = "GDP growth of origin (%)",
       y = "growth (0 = decline, 1 = growth)", colour = "Market")
```

About `r round(100 * mean(growth.data$growth))`% of all rows show growth, so the classes are not balanced. The share depends strongly on the year, since no market grew anywhere in 2020 and most almost all grew in 2022. In 2021, near markets already grew in about 73% of rows, far markets only in about 49%. Before covid the share was between about 47% and 73%, so in normal years many cantons grow while others decline.

When the origin economy shrank strongly (below about -4% for near and -1% for far markets), there was no growth. Above that, the curves go up and down between about 55% and 95% without a clear direction. So the link between GDP growth and growth comes mostly from the covid year, meaning year and covid are the main candidates for explaining growth.

## Origin markets
```{r eda-origin, fig.height = 3.5}
country_order <- hotel |>
  group_by(origin_group, origin_country) |>
  summarise(med = median(log_arrivals), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(origin_group), med) |>
  pull(origin_country)

hotel |>
  mutate(origin_country = factor(origin_country, levels = country_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(log_arrivals, origin_country, fill = origin_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_cols) +
  labs(x = "log(arrivals)", y = NULL, fill = "Market")
```
```{r med-germany, include=FALSE}
# median arrivals per canton and year for Germany (largest market)
med.germany <- median(hotel$arrivals[hotel$origin_country == "Germany"])
med.germany
```

Germany is by far the largest market, with a median of `r format(round(med.germany), big.mark = ",")` arrivals per canton and year. The other near markets follow, and the United States is the only far market at their level. The other far markets are smaller and have wider boxes. The origin market is clearly an important predictor.

## Cantons
```{r eda-canton, fig.height = 3.5}
hotel |>
  group_by(canton, origin_group) |>
  summarise(med = median(log_arrivals), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = origin_group, values_from = med) |>
  mutate(canton = reorder(canton, near)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = canton)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = far, xend = near, yend = canton), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(x = near, colour = "near"), size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(x = far,  colour = "far"),  size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  labs(x = "Median log(arrivals) per market", y = NULL, colour = "Market")
```
The gap between near and far markets is not the same in every canton. In Zurich, Bern, Lucerne and Obwalden far markets are as large as near markets. In Thurgau, Glarus, Jura and the two Appenzells far markets are much more absent. The differences between cantons look large, which suggests a canton × market group interaction. We test it in the models.

## Year

```{r eda-year, fig.height = 3.5}
national <- hotel |>
  group_by(year, origin_country, origin_group) |>
  summarise(arrivals = sum(arrivals), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(origin_country) |>
  mutate(index = 100 * arrivals / arrivals[year == 2019]) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(national, aes(year, index, group = origin_country, colour = origin_group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2025) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "National arrivals (2019 = 100)", colour = "Market")
```
Covid hit far markets much harder. Taken together, near markets fell to about half of their 2019 arrivals in 2020. Far markets fell to about 10 % and only got close to 2019 again in 2025, and they recovered very unevenly. The path over time is clearly not a straight line and differs between near and far markets.

## Exchange rate

```{r eda-fx, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(hotel, aes(real_fx_index, log_arrivals, colour = origin_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  labs(x = "Real exchange-rate index (2016 = 100)", y = "log(arrivals)", colour = "Market")
```
The exchange rate of near markets stays in a narrow range (about 97 to 109), while far market currencies move much more (about 65 to 113). For far markets, arrivals tend to be higher when the index is higher, but the curve is not a straight line and dips around 90 to 95. For near markets there is no clear pattern. A smooth curve for the exchange rate, separately for near and far markets, is worth trying in the models.

## GDP

```{r eda-gdp, fig.height = 3.5}
ggplot(hotel, aes(gdp_growth_origin, log_arrivals, colour = origin_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "gam", formula = y ~ s(x)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = group_cols) +
  labs(x = "Real GDP growth of origin country (%)", y = "log(arrivals)", colour = "Market")
```

For near markets the curve is fairly flat, highest around 0% and slightly lower at both ends. For far markets the curve goes up and down without a clear direction. GDP growth does not show a simple relationship with arrivals, which we check in the models.

## Collinearity

```{r vif}
lm.vif <- lm(log_arrivals ~ canton + origin_country + year + real_fx_index +
               log_beds + rel_income + gdp_growth_origin,
             data = hotel)
vif(lm.vif)
```
`log_beds` and `rel_income` have very high values (16.5 and 10.2, respectively). The number of beds barely changes over time within a canton, so it is almost the same information as `canton`. Relative income barely changes within a country, so it is almost the same as `origin_country`. We therefore do not put them in the same model, but rather each model uses either canton and origin country, or beds and relative income.

# Models

## Linear Model

Chaitanya Arya took the lead on this method.

The linear model is our reference model. It answers the question: how many more or fewer visitors does a canton get from a market, and how much of this is explained by time, the covid years, the exchange rate and the economy of the origin country? The response is `log_arrivals`, so each coefficient $b$ is read as a change of about $100 \cdot (e^{b} - 1)$ % in arrivals. Following the collinearity check, `log_beds` and `rel_income` are left out.

### Model building

We start with main effects only.

```{r lm-main}
lm.main <- lm(log_arrivals ~ canton + origin_country + year + covid_period +
                real_fx_index + gdp_growth_origin,
              data = hotel)

drop1(lm.main, test = "F") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "LM 1: F-test for dropping each term")
```

Canton, origin market, year and the covid period are clearly needed (R² = `r round(summary(lm.main)$r.squared, 2)`). The exchange rate and GDP growth are not significant once the origin market is in the model: most of the differences in the exchange rate are between countries, and those are already captured by `origin_country`.

The EDA showed that near and far markets reacted differently to covid and do not go to the same cantons. So in a second model we let the covid effect, the exchange-rate effect and the canton effect differ between near and far markets.

```{r lm-int}
lm.int <- lm(log_arrivals ~ canton + origin_country + year + covid_period +
               real_fx_index + gdp_growth_origin +
               origin_group:real_fx_index + origin_group:covid_period +
               canton:origin_group,
             data = hotel)

anova(lm.main, lm.int) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "LM 1 vs LM 2 (with near/far interactions)")
```

The interactions improve the model a lot (R² goes up to `r round(summary(lm.int)$r.squared, 2)`), so LM 2 is our final linear model.

### Interpretation

```{r lm-effects}
b <- coef(lm.int)
V <- vcov(lm.int)

# % change in arrivals with 95% CI; for far markets: main effect + interaction
pct_effect <- function(terms) {
  est <- sum(b[terms])
  se  <- sqrt(sum(V[terms, terms]))
  round(100 * (exp(est + c(-1.96, 0, 1.96) * se) - 1), 1)
}

effects <- rbind(
  "Year (+1)"                  = pct_effect("year"),
  "During covid, near markets" = pct_effect("covid_periodduring"),
  "During covid, far markets"  = pct_effect(c("covid_periodduring", "covid_periodduring:origin_groupfar")),
  "Post covid, near markets"   = pct_effect("covid_periodpost"),
  "Post covid, far markets"    = pct_effect(c("covid_periodpost", "covid_periodpost:origin_groupfar")),
  "FX index +1, near markets"  = pct_effect("real_fx_index"),
  "FX index +1, far markets"   = pct_effect(c("real_fx_index", "real_fx_index:origin_groupfar")),
  "GDP growth +1 pp"           = pct_effect("gdp_growth_origin")
)
colnames(effects) <- c("lower 95%", "% change", "upper 95%")
knitr::kable(effects, caption = "LM 2: effects on arrivals in %")
```

- **Trend:** with everything else fixed, arrivals grow by about `r effects["Year (+1)", 2]` % per year.
- **Covid:** in 2020-2021, near markets lost about two thirds of their arrivals, while far markets almost disappeared (`r effects["During covid, far markets", 2]` %). After covid (2022-2025), both are still below the pre-covid trend line, and far markets more so (`r effects["Post covid, far markets", 2]` % vs `r effects["Post covid, near markets", 2]` %). Because the yearly trend keeps adding about 11 % per year, this matches the EDA: near markets were back at their 2019 level by 2023, while far markets were still below it in 2024.
- **Exchange rate and GDP:** a 1-point stronger origin currency (in real terms) does not significantly change arrivals for either group, and one extra percentage point of GDP growth adds only about `r effects["GDP growth +1 pp", 2]` %. Within a market, these yearly changes matter much less than covid and the long-term trend.

The canton × origin group interaction shows where far markets go compared with near markets:

```{r lm-canton, fig.height = 5}
ci <- confint(lm.int)
k  <- grep("^canton.*:origin_groupfar$", names(b))
canton_far <- data.frame(
  canton = sub("^canton(.*):origin_groupfar$", "\\1", names(b)[k]),
  est    = 100 * (exp(b[k]) - 1),
  lower  = 100 * (exp(ci[k, 1]) - 1),
  upper  = 100 * (exp(ci[k, 2]) - 1)
)

ggplot(canton_far, aes(est, reorder(canton, est))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), colour = group_cols["far"]) +
  labs(x = "Extra % arrivals of far markets compared with near markets (vs Aargau)",
       y = NULL)
```

Compared with the reference canton Aargau, far markets are strongly over-represented in Bern, Obwalden, Lucerne, Zurich and Geneva, which are the classic Jungfrau, Titlis/Lake Lucerne and city destinations. Far markets are under-represented in Jura, Thurgau and Glarus. For a tourism agency, this means that money aimed at far markets is best spent on the cantons that already attract them, while smaller cantons depend mostly on near markets.

### Model checks

```{r lm-check, fig.height = 6}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(lm.int)
```

The residuals are centred around zero with fairly constant variance. The lower tail is heavier than normal. This comes mainly from the 25 rows with zero arrivals (small far markets in small cantons), which the log scale pulls far down.

### Cross-validation

```{r lm-cv, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(10)
n     <- nrow(hotel)
folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = n))

rmse.lm.main <- c()
rmse.lm.int  <- c()

for (k in 1:10) {
  hotel.train <- hotel[folds != k, ]
  hotel.test  <- hotel[folds == k, ]

  fit  <- lm(formula(lm.main), data = hotel.train)
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
  rmse.lm.main[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

  fit  <- lm(formula(lm.int), data = hotel.train)
  pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
  rmse.lm.int[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))
}

data.frame(model = c("LM 1: main effects", "LM 2: near/far interactions (final)"),
           mean_RMSE = c(mean(rmse.lm.main), mean(rmse.lm.int))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "10-fold CV, RMSE on log(arrivals)")
```

The interactions also help out of sample: the test RMSE drops from `r round(mean(rmse.lm.main), 2)` to `r round(mean(rmse.lm.int), 2)` on the log scale. The GAM section below compares this structure with non-linear smooths.

## Non-Linear Model: GAM

Laura Cunha took the lead on this method.

The LM assumes that time and the exchange rate affect log(arrivals) in a straight line. The GAM lets the data choose the shape, meaning the effects of year, exchange rate and GDP growth are smooth curves.

The GAM does not need the covid_period variable, since the year curves can follow each year separately, showing the covid drop and recovery directly.

Canton and origin market stay in the model as categories, so each canton and each market keeps its own level of arrivals. The smooth curves then show how arrivals change with year, exchange rate or GDP growth for the same canton and the same market, not differences between large and small destinations.

As in the linear model, log_beds and rel_income are left out because they are almost the same information as canton and origin market.

### Model building

We start GAM 1 with one smooth each for year, the real exchange rate and GDP growth of the origin country.

```{r gam-main}
gam.main <- gam(log_arrivals ~ canton + origin_country +
                  s(year, k = 10) + s(real_fx_index) + s(gdp_growth_origin),
                data = hotel)
```

The EDA showed that near and far markets went through covid very differently. So in GAM 2 the year and exchange-rate curves are fitted separately for near and far markets. `origin_group` adds nothing on top of `origin_country`. It is only needed because the curves are fitted for near/far markets with `by = origin_group`.

```{r gam-noint}
gam.noint <- gam(
  log_arrivals ~ canton + origin_group + origin_country +
    s(year, by = origin_group, k = 10) +
    s(real_fx_index, by = origin_group) +
    s(gdp_growth_origin),
  data = hotel
)
anova(gam.main, gam.noint, test = "F")
```

Separate curves improve the fit clearly. As in the linear model, GAM 3 lets each canton's level differ between near and far markets.

```{r gam-int}
gam.int <- gam(
  log_arrivals ~ canton * origin_group + origin_country +
    s(year, by = origin_group, k = 10) +
    s(real_fx_index, by = origin_group) +
    s(gdp_growth_origin),
  data = hotel
)
anova(gam.noint, gam.int, test = "F")
```

GAM 3 improves the fit again, and by more than the step from GAM 1 to GAM 2, so it is our final GAM. `year` has only 10 distinct values, so k = 10 is the most flexibility it can have.

GAM 3 explains `r round(100 * summary(gam.int)$dev.expl, 1)` % of the variation in log(arrivals) (adjusted R² = `r round(summary(gam.int)$r.sq, 3)`), almost the same as LM 2 (R² = `r round(summary(lm.int)$r.squared, 3)`). The smooth curves add little fit on top of the near/far interactions.

```{r gam-terms}
anova(gam.int)
```
`anova()` tests each term while keeping all the others in the model. The canton × market group interaction (`canton:origin_group`) is clearly significant (p < 2e-16), so far and near markets do not go to the same cantons. Because of this interaction, canton and market group both matter and are not interpreted on their own, due to the principle of marginality. The origin country also has a very strong effect.

All smooth terms show very strong evidence of an effect (p < 2e-16), except the exchange rate for near markets (edf 1.5, p = 0.38), meaning there is no evidence that it changes arrivals of near markets.

### Interpretation

```{r gam-final}
# smooth terms only; the full summary lists ~60 canton coefficients
summary(gam.int)$s.table |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r gam-smooths, fig.height = 7}
par(mfrow = c(3, 2))
plot(gam.int, select = 1, shade = TRUE, main = "Year, near markets")
plot(gam.int, select = 2, shade = TRUE, main = "Year, far markets")
plot(gam.int, select = 3, shade = TRUE, main = "Exchange rate, near markets")
plot(gam.int, select = 4, shade = TRUE, main = "Exchange rate, far markets")
plot(gam.int, select = 5, shade = TRUE, main = "GDP growth of origin")
```

Since the curves are on the log scale, a change on the y-axis is a percentage change in arrivals. A rise of 0.1 means about 10 % more arrivals, a rise of 1 means almost three times as many (e.g. from 1,000 to about 2,720), and a drop of 1 means about 63 % fewer (from 1,000 to about 370).

- **Year:** both curves are non-linear (edf 7.8 for near and 8.8 for far markets, with a maximum of 9), dropping sharply in 2020-2021 and then recovering. Compared with 2019, near markets recovered by 2023. Far markets, on the other hand, only got back to their 2019 level in 2025.
- **Exchange rate, near markets:** the curve is almost a straight line (edf 1.5) and not significant, meaning a stronger or weaker euro or pound within the observed range (index mostly between 99 and 108) does not change arrivals in a way we can detect.
- **Exchange rate, far markets:** the curve is rising overall but not steadily. Though significant, the low index values come from countries whose currencies lost value after 2020. So part of this curve may reflect slow post-covid recovery rather than the exchange rate itself. Therefore, we do not read it as a clear currency effect.
- **GDP growth:** the curve is very wiggly (edf about 9). Arrivals are lowest at GDP growth around -4 % and highest around 6 to 7 %. Because the curve goes up and down, we do not read it as a clear effect of the origin's economy.
- **Cantons:** the canton × group effects agree with the LM. Compared with Aargau, far markets are strongly over-represented in Bern, Obwalden, Lucerne, Zurich and Geneva, and under-represented in Jura, Thurgau and Glarus.

For the agency, the GAM tells the same story as the linear model: the differences between cantons and markets and the covid recovery matter much more than yearly changes in GDP growth. The one difference is the exchange rate for far markets, where the GAM finds a modest effect, so it is worth watching but not a main reason to shift the budget.

### Model checks

```{r gam-check, fig.height = 4.5}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
gam.check(gam.int)
```

- QQ-plot of the residuals (normality): most points lie on the line, but the lower tail falls clearly below it, so the residuals are not fully normal.
- Residuals vs linear predictor (mean zero, constant variance): the cloud is centred on 0. The spread is somewhat larger for small predicted values (small markets in small cantons). The diagonal line of points going down on the left comes from the 25 rows with zero arrivals.
- Histogram of the residuals (normality, second view): a roughly symmetric bell around 0, with a long tail to the left (same rows as in the QQ-plot).
- Response vs fitted values (overall fit): the points lie close to the diagonal, so the model fits well overall. The exception is the row of zero arrivals at the bottom, which the model predicts too high.

Overall the assumptions are reasonably met. The only clear problem is the zero-arrival rows, which the log scale pulls far down, as in the LM.

The k-index is slightly below 1 for all smooths. For `year`, `k` cannot be raised (only 10 distinct years). For GDP growth, a larger `k` would only make an already wiggly curve more flexible, which we do not need for interpretation.

### Cross-validation

We compare the three GAMs with the final linear model (LM 2) with repeated 10-fold cross-validation and report the RMSE on log(arrivals).

```{r gam-cv, cache = TRUE}

set.seed(10)
n <- nrow(hotel)
rmse.gam.main  <- c()
rmse.gam.noint <- c()
rmse.gam.int   <- c()
rmse.lm.rep  <- c()

for (i in 1:10) {
  # 1) prepare data: new random permutation each repetition
  inds.permuted  <- sample(1:n, replace = FALSE)
  hotel.permuted <- hotel[inds.permuted, ]
  folds <- cut(1:n, breaks = 10, labels = FALSE)

  rmse.fold.main  <- c()
  rmse.fold.noint <- c()
  rmse.fold.int   <- c()
  rmse.fold.lm    <- c()

  for (k in 1:10) {
    ind.test    <- which(folds == k)
    hotel.test  <- hotel.permuted[ind.test, ]
    hotel.train <- hotel.permuted[-ind.test, ]

    # 2) fit on train, 3) predict test, 4) compute RMSE
    fit  <- gam(formula(gam.main), data = hotel.train)
    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
    rmse.fold.main[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

    fit  <- gam(formula(gam.noint), data = hotel.train)
    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
    rmse.fold.noint[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

    fit  <- gam(formula(gam.int), data = hotel.train)
    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
    rmse.fold.int[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

    fit  <- lm(formula(lm.int), data = hotel.train)
    pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
    rmse.fold.lm[k] <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))
  }

  # average over 10 folds
  rmse.gam.main[i]  <- mean(rmse.fold.main)
  rmse.gam.noint[i] <- mean(rmse.fold.noint)
  rmse.gam.int[i]   <- mean(rmse.fold.int)
  rmse.lm.rep[i]    <- mean(rmse.fold.lm)
}
```

```{r gam-cv-results, fig.height = 3.5}
data.frame(
  model = c("GAM 1: main effects", "GAM 2: smooths by group",
               "GAM 3: + interaction (final)", "LM 2"),
  mean.RMSE = c(mean(rmse.gam.main), mean(rmse.gam.noint),
               mean(rmse.gam.int), mean(rmse.lm.rep))
) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Model", "Mean RMSE (log scale)"))

boxplot(rmse.gam.main, rmse.gam.noint, rmse.gam.int, rmse.lm.rep,
        names = c("GAM 1", "GAM 2", "GAM 3", "LM 2"),
        ylab = "Test RMSE")
```

GAM 3 has the lowest test RMSE (`r round(mean(rmse.gam.int), 2)` vs `r round(mean(rmse.lm.rep), 2)` for LM 2), and the boxes do not overlap, so the ranking does not depend on the split. On the log scale, an RMSE of `r round(mean(rmse.gam.int), 2)` means a typical prediction is off by a factor of about `r round(exp(mean(rmse.gam.int)), 1)`. The gain over LM 2 is small. The near/far interactions add much more than the smooth curves do.

Random folds test how well a model fills in a canton-market-year it has not seen. The agency will also want to know about the next years. As a check, we fit on 2016-2023 and predict 2024-2025 (80%/20% of the rows). With 8 training years, the year smooth can have at most `k = 8`.

```{r gam-time-split}
hotel.train <- hotel[hotel$year <= 2023, ]
hotel.test  <- hotel[hotel$year >= 2024, ]

f.time <- update(formula(gam.int), . ~ . - s(year, by = origin_group, k = 10) + s(year, by = origin_group, k = 8))

fit  <- gam(f.time, data = hotel.train)
pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
rmse.time.gam <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

fit  <- lm(formula(lm.int), data = hotel.train)
pred <- predict(fit, newdata = hotel.test)
rmse.time.lm <- sqrt(mean((hotel.test$log_arrivals - pred)^2))

data.frame(model = c("GAM 3", "LM 2"),
           RMSE  = c(rmse.time.gam, rmse.time.lm)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Train 2016-2023, test 2024-2025: RMSE")
```

Here the LM has the lower error (`r round(rmse.time.lm, 2)` vs `r round(rmse.time.gam, 2)`), so it predicts new years better than the GAM. With random folds it was the other way round (`r round(mean(rmse.lm.rep), 2)` vs `r round(mean(rmse.gam.int), 2)`). The GAM is therefore the better choice to describe the past ten years and the LM the better choice to predict the next ones.

## Generalized Linear Model (Binomial)

This section was lead by Benjamin Jud.

Using a Binomial Generalized Linear Model, we will attempt to model and predict growth from any specific country based market, with a focus on discovering the of impact economic metrics such as origin GDP gowtrh, foreign exchange rates, relative income, whether countries need visitor visas, and whether grouping near or far makes a difference.

The following is an overview of growth, where `1` represents a year-over-year increase in hotel stays from that particular country, and `0` represents a decline in hotel stays. To model this variable, we display the proportion of canton-origin market combinations which showed a year-over-year increase in growth.

```{r include=FALSE}
n_growth = tapply(swiss_hotel_panel$growth == 1, swiss_hotel_panel$year, sum, na.rm = TRUE)

yoy_growth = as.numeric(n_growth) / as.numeric(table(swiss_hotel_panel$year))
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
years = unique(swiss_hotel_panel$year)

plot(years, yoy_growth, type = "b", pch = 16,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Proportion of Canton-Country Combinations with YoY growth",
     xaxp = c(216, 2025, 1),
     main = "YoY Growth in Hotel Stays", xaxt = "n")

axis(1, at = years)
```

From 2016 to 2018 hotel growth was relatively stable, before slightly dipping in 2019 and achieving no growth in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. 2021 and 2022 lead with high growth rates, before rates stabilized at higher than pre-pandemic levels in 2023 to 2025.

First, we split our data into a training and testing set such that we can later run a prediction against the model, and validate our outcomes. We will be using a split of 70% (training) and 30% (testing).

```{r}

glm_sample_rows = sample.int(nrow(swiss_hotel_panel), floor(0.7 * nrow(swiss_hotel_panel)))

glm_train_dataset <- swiss_hotel_panel[glm_sample_rows, ]   
glm_test_dataset  <- swiss_hotel_panel[-glm_sample_rows, ]  
```

Next, we will construct a binomial GLM Model to find factors that contribute to this growth.

```{r}
##not sure how many vars you can include in one of these
glm.growth = glm(growth ~ 
                  gdp_growth_origin
                 +real_fx_index
                 +rel_income
                 +visa_required
                 +origin_group,
                 data = glm_train_dataset,
                 family = 'binomial')
summary(glm.growth)
```

Through the model summary call, four of five economic indicators (`gdp_growth_origin`, `real_fx_index`, `rel_income`, & `visa_required`) showed statistical significance.

```{r echo=FALSE}

coef_table = data.frame(
  "Predictive_Variable" = colnames(glm.growth$model)[-1][-5],
  Coefficient = coef(glm.growth)[-1][-5],
  "Odds" = exp(coef(glm.growth)[-1][-5]),
  "Odds_Percent_Increase" = (exp(coef(glm.growth)[-1][-5])-1) *100,
  row.names   = NULL
)
coef_table

```

The `odds` column represents the exponentially transformed coefficient, where a single unit increase in the predictive variable creates an increase in the odds of hotels having growth from any particular origin market. `Odds_Percent_Increase` represents the percent increase on growth if the predictive value were to change.

In this model, `rel_income` shows the odds by a significant margin, followed by `gpd_growth_origin`, while `real_fx_index` slightly reduces growth, and `visa_required` significantly reduces growth.

```{r include=FALSE}
## this block does not print in the knitted version, just for calculation & transparency
indian_median = median(swiss_hotel_panel$rel_income[swiss_hotel_panel$origin_country == "India"])
indian_median
```

Relative income, which is defined as any countries median income compared to the Swiss income (controlled for exchange rates and year), is an interesting factor to review in this model, as the countries selected in this analysis all have lower incomes than Switzerland. While certain developed nations have higher relative income, India has a relative income to Switzerland of just 9.28% (median) across the measured time period.

#### Predicting Growth from Origin Country GDP Growth

```{r}
glm.growth_origin = glm(growth~gdp_growth_origin, data = glm_train_dataset, family = 'binomial')
summary(glm.growth_origin)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}

glm_origin_growth_predict_response = predict(glm.growth_origin, newdata = glm_train_dataset, type = "response")
b = coef(glm.growth_origin)
intercept_50p = -b[1] / b[2]

plot(glm_train_dataset$gdp_growth_origin,
     jitter(glm_train_dataset$growth, amount = 0.03),
     pch = 16, 
     col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3),
     xlab = "Origin Country GDP Growth (%)", 
     ylab = "Growth in Swiss Hotels")
title("Visitors come to Switzerland when their Country is Growing")

ord = order(glm_train_dataset$gdp_growth_origin)
lines(
  glm_train_dataset$gdp_growth_origin[ord],
  glm_origin_growth_predict_response[ord],
  col = "red",
  lwd = 3
)
#abline(h = 0.5)
#abline(v = intercept_50p)

 #vert segmewnt
segments(
  x0 = intercept_50p, y0 = -2,
  x1 = intercept_50p, y1 = 0.5,
  lty = 2, col = "gray20"
)

#horiz segment
segments( 
  x0 = -12, y0 = 0.5,
  x1 = intercept_50p, y1 = 0.5,
  lty = 2, col = "gray20"
)


print(paste("Origin GPD Growth at 50%:", round(-b[1] / b[2], 3), 
            "Log-Odds:", round(exp(b[2]), 3)))

```

While looking at the chart, it may seem like there is not a large impact of origin country GDP growth on resulting growth among Swiss hotels for visitors from that particular country. For a 50% chance in hotel growth, the corresponding country shows growth of just 0.108%. Reviewing the coefficient of the GLM Binomial model, once transformed by the exponential, yields 1.218. This can be interpreted that a one percent increase in the GDP of the origin country, adds 21.8% increase in likelihood of growth of overnight stays by visitors of that particular country.

Hotel management staff, should focus on attracting visitors from markets which are growing, even if at minimal rates. Additionally, there is higher growth likelihoods which can be found by the hotels if they focus on attracting markets which are experiencing higher rates of growth.

## Support Vector Machine

The binomial GLM above asks whether a market grows in a canton from one year to the next. Here we ask the same question with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) and compare the two on the same data. An SVM does not give coefficients or probabilities. It looks for the boundary between "growth" and "decline" rows with the widest possible margin. Only the rows on or inside the margin (the support vectors) define this boundary. A radial kernel allows the boundary to be curved.

### Data and set-up

The response is `growth` as a factor ("decline"/"growth"). For a fair comparison, the SVM uses the same five predictors as the GLM: GDP growth of the origin, real exchange rate, relative income, visa requirement and near/far market. `svm()` scales all predictors by default (`scale = TRUE`). This matters because the SVM works with distances and without scaling the exchange-rate index (around 100) would dominate GDP growth (a few %).

```{r svm-prep}

svm.data <- hotel |>
  filter(!is.na(growth)) |>
  mutate(growth = factor(growth, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("decline", "growth"))) |>
  select(year, growth, gdp_growth_origin, real_fx_index, rel_income,
         visa_required, origin_group, canton) |>
  as.data.frame()

set.seed(10)
svm.ind   <- createDataPartition(svm.data$growth, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
svm.train <- svm.data[svm.ind, ]
svm.test  <- svm.data[-svm.ind, ]

f.svm    <- growth ~ gdp_growth_origin + real_fx_index + rel_income +
                     visa_required + origin_group

f.canton <- update(f.svm, . ~ . + canton)

n.cells <- nrow(distinct(svm.data, gdp_growth_origin, real_fx_index, rel_income,
                         visa_required, origin_group))

nir <- max(prop.table(table(svm.data$growth)))
```

`r round(100 * nir)`% of the rows show growth, so a model that always says "growth" is already right `r round(100 * nir)`% of the time (No Information Rate). Any useful model must beat this value.

The five predictors only change between origin countries and years, not between cantons. All `r nrow(svm.data)` rows therefore have only `r n.cells` different predictor values (12 markets × 10 years). Within one market and year some cantons grow and others decline, but the model sees the same input for all of them and must give them the same prediction.

### Model building and cross-validation

We compare three SVMs with 10-fold cross-validation on the training set. `tune()` fits each model for every combination of the values in `ranges` and keeps the one with the lowest CV error, meaning the share of misclassified rows. The same seed before each `tune()` gives the same folds, so the three models are compared on the same data.

- **SVM 1, linear kernel:** a straight boundary, like the GLM. The cost C is tuned and a large C makes every margin violation expensive, with a narrow margin, few support vectors and risk of overfitting. A small C gives a wide margin and a simpler model.
- **SVM 2, radial kernel:** a curved boundary, with C and gamma are tuned together. A large gamma means each support vector only influences rows very close to it, which allows a very wiggly boundary.
- **SVM 3, radial kernel + canton:** canton is the only predictor that changes within a market and year, so it could separate cantons that the other predictors cannot.

```{r svm-tune, cache = TRUE}
set.seed(10)
tune.lin <- tune(svm, f.svm, data = svm.train, kernel = "linear",
                 ranges = list(cost = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)))
set.seed(10)
tune.rad <- tune(svm, f.svm, data = svm.train, kernel = "radial",
                 ranges = list(cost = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100), gamma = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)))
set.seed(10)
tune.can <- tune(svm, f.canton, data = svm.train, kernel = "radial",
                 ranges = list(cost = c(1, 10, 100), gamma = c(0.01, 0.1, 1)))

svm.lin <- tune.lin$best.model
svm.rad <- tune.rad$best.model
svm.can <- tune.can$best.model
```

```{r svm-cv-table}

c("SVM 1: linear"          = tune.lin$best.performance,
  "SVM 2: radial"          = tune.rad$best.performance,
  "SVM 3: radial + canton" = tune.can$best.performance) |>
  round(3)
```

The CV accuracy is 1 minus the error:

- **SVM 1** reaches a CV accuracy of `r round(100 * (1 - tune.lin$best.performance))`%, only a little above always guessing "growth". `r svm.lin$tot.nSV` of the `r nrow(svm.train)` training rows (`r round(100 * svm.lin$tot.nSV / nrow(svm.train))`%) are support vectors. So most rows lie on or inside the margin: growth and decline rows overlap strongly and a straight boundary cannot separate them.
- **SVM 2** is clearly the best (`r round(100 * (1 - tune.rad$best.performance))`%). It needs a large gamma (`r tune.rad$best.parameters$gamma`), meaning a very wiggly boundary. With only `r n.cells` predictor values, this lets the SVM recognise each market-year and predict what most cantons did in it. It learns which market-years grew, not a general rule.
- **SVM 3** is worse than SVM 2 (`r round(100 * (1 - tune.can$best.performance))`%). Canton adds 25 dummy variables but whether a market grows in a given year is mostly the same across cantons, so it does not help to predict the direction of growth.

SVM 2 is our final SVM. Its best C (`r tune.rad$best.parameters$cost`) is at the edge of the grid and, since a large C means a narrower margin and more risk of overfitting, we do not tune further.

The two plots below show the boundary of SVM 1 and SVM 2 for GDP growth and exchange rate. The SVM uses five predictors but a plot can only show two, so the other three are fixed at typical values (median relative income, no visa and near market). Crosses are support vectors, circles the other rows and the colour of the area is the predicted class.

```{r svm-regions, fig.height = 5, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%"}
slice.typ <- list(rel_income    = median(svm.train$rel_income),
                  visa_required = 0, origin_group = "near")
plot(svm.lin, svm.train, gdp_growth_origin ~ real_fx_index, slice = slice.typ)
plot(svm.rad, svm.train, gdp_growth_origin ~ real_fx_index, slice = slice.typ)
```

SVM 1 (left) draws one straight boundary, like the GLM. But the GLM's line lies higher. At an exchange-rate index of 100, for instance, the GLM predicts "decline" below about 0 % GDP growth, while SVM 1 only below about -3 %. So the GLM predicts "decline" more often, which explains its higher specificity. SVM 2 (right) predicts "decline" in separate islands, since it recognises single market-years. The wiggly boundary comes from the large gamma. The fixed values create combinations that do not exist in the data, so the plots show the shape of the boundary rather than real predictions.

### Comparison with the GLM on the test set

To compare the GLM with the SVMs on the same rows, we refit the GLM from the previous section on the SVM training set and predict the same test set. For the GLM, a fitted probability above 0.5 counts as "growth". The output below first shows the test-set accuracy of all three models, then the full confusion matrix of the final model, SVM 2. "Growth" is the positive class, so sensitivity is the share of growing rows found, and specificity is the share of declining rows found.

```{r svm-test}
# glm treats the first factor level ("decline") as 0 and "growth" as 1
glm.svm.split <- glm(f.svm, family = binomial, data = svm.train)

# predict() only uses the predictors from the formula, the growth column in
# svm.test is ignored (= test_in); svm.test$growth is the truth (= test_truth)
pred.glm <- factor(ifelse(predict(glm.svm.split, svm.test, type = "response") > 0.5,
                          "growth", "decline"), levels = c("decline", "growth"))
pred.lin <- predict(svm.lin, svm.test)
pred.rad <- predict(svm.rad, svm.test)

# positive = "growth", otherwise caret uses the first level ("decline")
confusion.matrix.glm <- confusionMatrix(pred.glm, svm.test$growth, positive = "growth")
confusion.matrix.lin <- confusionMatrix(pred.lin, svm.test$growth, positive = "growth")
confusion.matrix.rad <- confusionMatrix(pred.rad, svm.test$growth, positive = "growth")

# accuracy of the three models side by side
cat("Test-set accuracy\n")
c("GLM" = confusion.matrix.glm$overall[["Accuracy"]],
  "SVM 1: linear" = confusion.matrix.lin$overall[["Accuracy"]],
  "SVM 2: radial" = confusion.matrix.rad$overall[["Accuracy"]]) |>
  round(3)

# full output for final SVM
cat("\nConfusion matrix of SVM 2 on the test set\n")
confusion.matrix.rad
```

On the test set SVM 2 is right `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.rad$overall["Accuracy"], 1)`% of the time, against `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.glm$overall["Accuracy"], 1)`% for the GLM, `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.lin$overall["Accuracy"], 1)`% for SVM 1 and `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.glm$overall["AccuracyNull"], 1)`% for always guessing "growth" (No Information Rate). The GLM finds `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.glm$byClass["Sensitivity"])`% of the growing rows but only `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.glm$byClass["Specificity"])`% of the declines and SVM 1 only `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.lin$byClass["Specificity"])`%, meaning they mostly predict "growth". SVM 2 finds `r round(100 * confusion.matrix.rad$byClass["Specificity"])`% of the declines, so it is better at warning about a decline. Kappa, which measures the improvement over chance, confirms it with `r round(confusion.matrix.rad$overall["Kappa"], 2)` for SVM 2 and only `r round(confusion.matrix.glm$overall["Kappa"], 2)` for the GLM.

The next plot shows where this difference comes from, through the share of test rows with growth per year, observed and predicted.

```{r svm-year, fig.height = 3.5}
# share of rows with growth per year: observed, GLM and SVM 2
data.frame(year     = svm.test$year,
           Observed = svm.test$growth == "growth",
           GLM      = pred.glm == "growth",
           `SVM 2`  = pred.rad == "growth",
           check.names = FALSE) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "source", values_to = "growth") |>
  group_by(year, source) |>
  summarise(share = mean(growth), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, colour = source, linetype = source)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(GLM = "grey50", Observed = "black", `SVM 2` = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(GLM = 2, Observed = 1, `SVM 2` = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2016:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of rows with growth", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

Both models catch 2020, when GDP fell in every origin country. The difference lies in the recovery. The GLM predicts growth everywhere in 2021, when only about 60% of rows grew, and is clearly off from 2023 on. The SVM follows the observed line closely in 2021 and 2022 but moves away from it from 2023 on. In 2024 and 2025 both models again predict growth for about 90 % of rows or more, while only about 65% grew. The same happens before covid. This is a limit of the predictors. Within one market and year the cantons split and since all of them get the same input, a model can only predict what most of them did.

So the SVM's advantage does not come from a better economic rule. It recognises each market-year from its unique combination of GDP growth, exchange rate and income, and learns what happened in it.

### Cross-validation: GLM vs SVM

The test set above is only one split, so one (un)lucky split can favour one model. We therefore also compare the GLM, SVM 1 and SVM 2 with 10-fold cross-validation on the whole data. All three models use the same folds, so in each fold they are trained and tested on the same rows. Cost and gamma are kept from `tune()`.

```{r svm-cv-glm, cache = TRUE, fig.height = 3.5}
# the test set above is only ONE split, and one (un)lucky split can favour one
# model. So we also compare the models over 10 different splits (folds).
# All models use the SAME folds: in each fold they are trained and tested on
# the same rows, so differences come from the models, not from the rows.
# Tuning values (cost, gamma) are kept from tune() above.

set.seed(10)
n <- nrow(svm.data)
svm.data.perm <- svm.data[sample(1:n), ]          
folds <- cut(1:n, breaks = 10, labels = FALSE)    

acc.glm <- c()
acc.lin <- c()
acc.rad <- c()

for (k in 1:10) {
  cv.test  <- svm.data.perm[folds == k, ]
  cv.train <- svm.data.perm[folds != k, ]

  # GLM: probability > 0.5 -> growth
  fit  <- glm(f.svm, family = binomial, data = cv.train)
  pred <- ifelse(predict(fit, cv.test, type = "response") > 0.5, "growth", "decline")
  acc.glm[k] <- mean(pred == cv.test$growth)

  # SVM 1: linear
  fit  <- svm(f.svm, data = cv.train, kernel = "linear",
              cost = tune.lin$best.parameters$cost)
  acc.lin[k] <- mean(predict(fit, cv.test) == cv.test$growth)

  # SVM 2: radial
  fit  <- svm(f.svm, data = cv.train, kernel = "radial",
              cost  = tune.rad$best.parameters$cost,
              gamma = tune.rad$best.parameters$gamma)
  acc.rad[k] <- mean(predict(fit, cv.test) == cv.test$growth)
}

# mean accuracy over the 10 folds
c("GLM (binomial)" = mean(acc.glm),
  "SVM 1: linear"  = mean(acc.lin),
  "SVM 2: radial"  = mean(acc.rad)) |>
  round(3)

# spread over the folds: does the ranking depend on the split?
boxplot(acc.glm, acc.lin, acc.rad,
        names = c("GLM", "SVM 1: linear", "SVM 2: radial"),
        ylab = "Accuracy per fold")
abline(h = mean(svm.data$growth == "growth"), lty = 2)   # always "growth"
```

Over the 10 folds, SVM 2 reaches a mean accuracy of `r round(100 * mean(acc.rad), 1)`% against `r round(100 * mean(acc.glm), 1)` % for the GLM and `r round(100 * mean(acc.lin), 1)`% for SVM 1. SVM 2 is better than the GLM in `r sum(acc.rad > acc.glm)` of 10 folds, so the ranking from the test set does not depend on the split. The GLM and the linear SVM are again almost equal, meaning the gain comes from the curved boundary, not from using an SVM. The CV accuracy of SVM 2 is slightly optimistic because cost and gamma were tuned on part of the same rows.

### Predicting future years

The random split tests market-years that the model has already seen in other cantons. The agency wants to know about next year, which no model has seen. As in the GAM section, we fit on 2016-2023 and predict 2024-2025.

```{r svm-time}
svm.train.t <- svm.data[svm.data$year <= 2023, ]
svm.test.t  <- svm.data[svm.data$year >= 2024, ]

fit.glm.t <- glm(f.svm, family = binomial, data = svm.train.t)
fit.lin.t <- svm(f.svm, data = svm.train.t, kernel = "linear",
                 cost = tune.lin$best.parameters$cost)
fit.rad.t <- svm(f.svm, data = svm.train.t, kernel = "radial",
                 cost = tune.rad$best.parameters$cost, gamma = tune.rad$best.parameters$gamma)

acc.t <- c(
  "Always 'growth'" = mean(svm.test.t$growth == "growth"),
  "GLM (binomial)"  = mean(ifelse(predict(fit.glm.t, svm.test.t, type = "response") > 0.5,
                                  "growth", "decline") == svm.test.t$growth),
  "SVM 1: linear"   = mean(predict(fit.lin.t, svm.test.t) == svm.test.t$growth),
  "SVM 2: radial"   = mean(predict(fit.rad.t, svm.test.t) == svm.test.t$growth)
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Accuracy = acc.t), digits = 3,
             caption = "Train 2016-2023, test 2024-2025")
```

For future years no model beats always guessing "growth" (`r round(100 * acc.t[1])`%). SVM 1 gives exactly the same accuracy because it predicts "growth" for every row. SVM 2 is the worst (`r round(100 * acc.t["SVM 2: radial"])`%), suggesting its wiggly boundary learned the past market-years by heart and does not carry over to new ones. This is the same lesson as for the GAM: the flexible model describes the past best but it is not the safer model for the future.

### Conclusion SVM vs GLM

- The radial SVM classifies growth clearly better than the GLM on market-years it has seen, both on the test set and in all 10 CV folds, and it finds more of the declines.
- For new years, neither the SVM nor the GLM predicts the direction of growth better than always guessing "growth". Whether a market grows depends mostly on what happens in a given year, such as covid, and in normal years it differs between cantons. The economic indicators move together with such shocks (GDP fell in 2020), but they do not announce them in advance, so they cannot forecast growth for a new year.
- For the agency, the GLM remains the model to explain growth, since its coefficients can be read, while both models show that GDP growth, exchange rate and income alone are not enough to forecast it.
